6.1.name: 6.01.md
6.1.text:
A parameter is a constituent part of a function's definition. It is the part that defines the number and type of argument(s) a function call might take. In the function's definition (or declaration) it comes after the function's name and is enclosed inside parentheses. A function could also have a void parameter, i.e. it takes no arguments.

An argument is the initializer for a function's parameter. When a function is called, through the call operator (), an argument or a list of arguments is passed through it to initialize the value of it's parameters. All initialization are local in scope and last the lifetime of the function. The type and number of arguments must match the type and number of arguments of the parameters used to define the function.

6.6.name: 6.06.md
6.6.text:
A parameter defines the number and type of argument a function might take. It is part of a function's declaration.

A local variable is an automatic object, which is defined and initialized through the function's parameters or in the function's body. Its scope is limited to the function's call. In other words, it is created when the function is called and destroyed when the function returns.

A static variable is an object that is defined within the function's body. It, too, is local in scope variable; however, it is initialized once only, when the function is called for the first time, and its value persists until it is reassigned by a subsequent call.

6.13.text: void f(T) is a pass by value function that copies an object of type T locally and uses it as its argument, while void f(T&) is pass by reference function that accepts a reference to a type T object as its argument, no copying is involved.

6.14.name: 6.14.md
6.14.text: Whenever we are passing a large object to a function we should use pass by reference to avoid the overhead of copying. When need to perform changes to a parameter without changing the original value of the argument passed, we should use pass by value.

6.34.text:
```text
if (val != 0)
```

The recursion would work fine for 0 and positive integers. However, if we mistakenly passed a negative integer to factorial, val != 0 will not terminate the recursion (and return 1); it will keep going until the stack is overflown. Since the factorial of a negative number is undefined we should use val > 1 instead.

6.35.name: 6.35.md
6.35.text:
Because the postfix decrement operator yields an unchanged value of its operand , and thereafter, increments it. This means the value of val will be unmodified on each recursive call, which would lead to an infinite recursion.

Using the prefix decrement to solve the recursion issue is equally problematic because it would have a side effect on the value of val on the right-hand side of the multiplication operator when the function returns. The side effect could be demonstrated as follows:

```cpp
<returned value from recursive call> * val - 1;
```

6.49.name: 6.49.md
6.49.text: A candidate function is an overloaded function whose name is identified by the compiler as match for the name of a given function call. A viable function is a candidate function that has the same number of parameters as the number of arguments passed in the function call of an overloaded function.

6.50.name: 6.50.md
6.50.text:
```text
(a) f(2.56, 42)
(b) f(42)
(c) f(42, 0)
(d) f(2.56, 3.14)
```

Candidate functions:

```cpp
void f();
void f(int);
void f(int, int);
void f(double, double = 3.14);
```

(a) ambiguous: both f(int, int) and f(double, double = 3.14) are viable

```cpp
functions; however, neither is an overall "best match" because both have one
parameter that is an exact match of the argument passed and one that is a match
through a built-in conversion, a "lesser" match.
```

(b) f(int) is the best match from the candidate functions. It has the same

```text
number of parameters as the argument passed and the exact match of its type.
```

(c) f(int, int) is the best match.

(d) f(double, double = 3.14) is a best match.

6.53.name: 6.53.md
6.53.text:
```cpp
(a) int calc(int&, int&);
	int calc(const int&, const int&);
(b) int calc(char*, char*);
	int calc(const char*, const char*);
(c) int calc(char*, char*);
	int calc(char* const, char* const);
```

(a) calc is overloaded on low-level const. The compiler will use the

```text
'constness' of the argument in the call to these functions to determine the
best match. If both arguments are non-constant references then cal(int&,
int&) will be called, on the other hand, if the arguments are constant
references than calc(const int&, const int&) will be called. If one
argument is a const and the other is non-constant int &, the compiler will
return an error, because the call is ambiguous.
```

(b) The same as a applies in regards to function matching through const

```text
conversion, but parameters' types are a pointer to character.
```

(c) Illegal: ambiguous. Here, the parameters' type in the first declaration is

```text
pointer to a char, while in the second it is const pointer to a char, which
is a top-level const. In function matching, top-level constants are
discarded, and thus, we end up with the same definition: a function that
takes pointer to char and returns an int.
```
